# What are the methods to prevent rusting of iron? ![Flexi Avatar](/flexi/flexi-full-circle.svg) Flexi Says: There are several methods to prevent rusting of iron: 1. **Galvanization:** This process involves the coating of iron or steel with a thin layer of zinc. The zinc prevents water and oxygen from coming in direct contact with the iron, thus preventing rusting. 2. **Painting or oiling:** A layer of paint or oil can be applied to the surface of iron to prevent it from coming into contact with water or air. 3. **Alloying:** Iron can be alloyed with other metals such as chromium, nickel, etc. to increase its resistance against rust. The common example of this is stainless steel. 4. **Sacrificial protection:** It involves attaching a more reactive metal such as magnesium to the iron. This more reactive metal will corrode before the iron does, thus protecting the iron from rusting. 5. **Barrier protection:** Physical barriers like plastic or metal foils can be used to prevent oxygen and water from reaching iron. 6. **Hot-dip galvanizing:** It consists of immersing the iron or steel in a bath of molten zinc. 7. **Applying Anodic protections:** Known as a method to control the corrosion of a metal surface by making it an anode of an electrolytic cell. All these methods essentially aim at preventing the iron from coming into contact with water and oxygen, which are essential for rusting to occur. # Explain the electrochemical theory of rusting of iron.

![Flexi Avatar](/flexi/flexi-full-circle.svg)

Flexi Says:

The electrochemical theory of rusting describes the process in which iron reacts with water and oxygen to form rust, which is a form of iron(III) oxide. The reaction is electrochemical in nature as it involves a transfer of electrons.

When iron comes into contact with water or moist air or an aqueous environment, it undergoes a redox reaction. Two distinct electrochemical reactions occur in the overall rusting process.

**1. Anodic Reaction:**

At the anode, iron gets oxidized by losing electrons and is transformed into iron(II) ions.

@$\begin{align\*}Fe(s) ⟶ Fe\end{align\*}@$2+ + 2e-

**2. Cathodic Reaction:**

Simultaneously, at the cathode, oxygen from the air or water gains electrons to be reduced by reacting with water (moisture) to form hydroxide (OH-) ions.

@$\begin{align\*}O\end{align\*}@$2(g) + 2H2O(l) + 4e- ⟶ 4OH-

These iron(II) ions then further react with the formed hydroxide ions to form a greenish precipitate which is iron(II) hydroxide (Fe(OH)2).

@$\begin{align\*}Fe\end{align\*}@$2+ + 2OH- ⟶ Fe(OH)2

But the tendency of iron(II) hydroxide (Fe(OH)2) is to undergo oxidation in the presence of dissolved oxygen from the air to form hydrated iron(III) oxide (Fe2O3.xH2O) or rust.

@$\begin{align\*}4Fe(OH)\end{align\*}@$2 + O2 + 2H2O ⟶ 4Fe(OH)3

@$\begin{align\*}Fe(OH)\end{align\*}@$3 ⟶ Fe2O3.xH2O (Rust)

The rusting of iron is an electrochemical process involving the formation of a weak anode and a cathode on the surface of the iron, in the presence of water and air, leading to the formation of rust.

**Rust** is a mixture of [iron oxides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_oxide "Iron oxide") formed by the reaction of [iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron "Iron") and [oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen "Oxygen") in the [catalytic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalytic "Catalytic") presence of [water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water "Water") or [air moisture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_moisture "Air moisture"), ranging in color from [red-orange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vermilion "Vermilion") to reddish-brown. The chemical composition consists of [iron(III) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron(III)_oxide "Iron(III) oxide") (Fe2O3), various [hydrous ferric oxides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron(III)_oxide#Hydrated_iron(III)_oxides "Iron(III) oxide") (Fe2O3·nH2O) and [iron(III) oxide-hydroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron(III)_oxide-hydroxide "Iron(III) oxide-hydroxide") (FeO(OH). It is typically associated with the [corrosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corrosion "Corrosion") of [refined iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refined_iron "Refined iron").

Given sufficient time, any iron mass in the presence of water and oxygen will form rust and could eventually convert entirely to rust. Surface rust is commonly flaky and [friable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friable "Friable"), and provides no [passivational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passivation_(chemistry) "Passivation (chemistry)") protection to the underlying iron unlike other metals such as aluminum, [copper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper "Copper"), and [tin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tin "Tin") which form stable oxide layers. *Rusting* is the common term for [corrosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corrosion "Corrosion") of elemental iron and [its alloys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferroalloy "Ferroalloy") such as [steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steel "Steel"). Many other [metals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metal "Metal") undergo similar corrosion, but the resulting oxides are not commonly called "rust".[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Several forms of rust are distinguishable both visually and by [spectroscopy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectroscopy "Spectroscopy"), and form under different circumstances.[[2]](#cite_note-2) Other forms of rust include the result of reactions between iron and [chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chloride "Chloride") in an environment deprived of oxygen. [Rebar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebar "Rebar") used in underwater [concrete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concrete "Concrete") [pillars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Column "Column"), which generates [green rust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_rust "Green rust"), is an example. Although rusting is generally a negative aspect of iron, a particular form of rusting, known as *stable rust*, causes the object to have a thin coating of rust over the top; this results from reaction with atmospheric oxygen. If kept free of moisture, it makes the "stable" layer protective to the iron below, albeit not to the extent of other oxides such as [aluminium oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium_oxide "Aluminium oxide") on [aluminium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium "Aluminium").[[3]](#cite_note-3)

## Chemical reactions

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Rust&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Chemical reactions")]

Rust is a general name for a complex of oxides and hydroxides of iron,[[4]](#cite_note-4) which occur when iron or some alloys that contain iron are exposed to oxygen and moisture for a long period of time. Over time, the oxygen combines with the metal, forming new compounds collectively called rust, in a process called rusting. Rusting is an [oxidation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redox "Redox") reaction specifically occurring with iron. Other metals also corrode via similar oxidation, but such corrosion is not called rusting.

The main [catalyst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalysis "Catalysis") for the rusting process is water. Iron or steel structures might appear to be solid, but water molecules can penetrate the microscopic [pits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitting_corrosion "Pitting corrosion") and cracks in any exposed metal. The hydrogen atoms present in water molecules can combine with other elements to form acids, which will eventually cause more metal to be exposed. If chloride ions are present, as is the case with saltwater, the corrosion is likely to occur more quickly. Meanwhile, the oxygen atoms combine with metallic atoms to form the destructive oxide compound. These iron compounds are brittle and crumbly and replace strong metallic iron, reducing the strength of the object.

### Oxidation of iron

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Rust&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Oxidation of iron")]

When iron is in contact with water and oxygen, it rusts.[[5]](#cite_note-Bodner-5) If [salt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt "Salt") is present, for example in [seawater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seawater "Seawater") or [salt spray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_spray "Salt spray"), the iron tends to rust more quickly, as a result of chemical reactions. Iron metal is relatively unaffected by pure water or by dry oxygen. As with other metals, like aluminium, a tightly adhering oxide coating, a [passivation layer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passivation_(chemistry) "Passivation (chemistry)"), protects the bulk iron from further oxidation. The conversion of the passivating [ferrous oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrous_oxide "Ferrous oxide") layer to rust results from the combined action of two agents, usually oxygen and water.

Other degrading solutions are [sulfur dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfur_dioxide "Sulfur dioxide") in water and [carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide "Carbon dioxide") in water. Under these corrosive conditions, [iron hydroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_hydroxide "Iron hydroxide") species are formed. Unlike ferrous oxides, the hydroxides do not adhere to the bulk metal. As they form and flake off from the surface, fresh iron is exposed, and the corrosion process continues until either all of the iron is consumed or all of the oxygen, water, carbon dioxide or sulfur dioxide in the system are removed or consumed.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

When iron rusts, the oxides take up more volume than the original metal; this expansion can generate enormous forces, damaging structures made with iron. See *[economic effect](#Economic_effect)* for more details.

### Associated reactions

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Rust&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Associated reactions")]

The rusting of iron is an electrochemical process that begins with the transfer of [electrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron "Electron") from iron to oxygen.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The iron is the reducing agent (gives up electrons) while the oxygen is the oxidizing agent (gains electrons). The rate of corrosion is affected by water and accelerated by [electrolytes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrolyte "Electrolyte"), as illustrated by the effects of [road salt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_salt "Road salt") on the corrosion of automobiles. The key reaction is the reduction of oxygen:

:   O2 + 4  *e*− + 2 [H2O](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water "Water") → 4  [OH−](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydroxide "Hydroxide")

Because it forms [hydroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydroxide "Hydroxide") [ions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ion "Ion"), this process is strongly affected by the presence of acid. Likewise, the corrosion of most metals by oxygen is accelerated at low [pH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PH "PH"). Providing the electrons for the above reaction is the oxidation of iron that may be described as follows:

:   Fe → Fe2+ + 2  *e*−

The following [redox reaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redox_reaction "Redox reaction") also occurs in the presence of water and is crucial to the formation of rust:

:   4 Fe2+ + O2 → 4 Fe3+ + 2 O2−

In addition, the following multistep [acid–base reactions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acid–base_reaction "Acid–base reaction") affect the course of rust formation:

:   Fe2+ + 2  H2O ⇌ Fe(OH)2 + 2  [H+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydron "Hydron")
:   Fe3+ + 3  H2O ⇌ Fe(OH)3 + 3  [H+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydron "Hydron")

as do the following [dehydration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dehydration_reaction "Dehydration reaction") equilibria:

:   [Fe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron "Iron")(OH)2 ⇌ FeO + [H2O](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water "Water")
:   [Fe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron "Iron")(OH)3 ⇌ FeO(OH) + [H2O](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water "Water")
:   2 FeO(OH) ⇌ Fe2O3 + [H2O](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water "Water")

From the above equations, it is also seen that the corrosion products are dictated by the availability of water and oxygen. With limited dissolved oxygen, iron(II)-containing materials are favoured, including [FeO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron(II)_oxide "Iron(II) oxide") and black [lodestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lodestone "Lodestone") or [magnetite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetite "Magnetite") (Fe3O4). High oxygen concentrations favour [ferric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferric "Ferric") materials with the nominal formulae Fe(OH)3−*x*O*x*⁄2. The nature of rust changes with time, reflecting the slow rates of the reactions of solids.[[5]](#cite_note-Bodner-5)

Furthermore, these complex processes are affected by the presence of other ions, such as [Ca2+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcium "Calcium"), which serve as electrolytes which accelerate rust formation, or combine with the [hydroxides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydroxide "Hydroxide") and [oxides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxide "Oxide") of iron to precipitate a variety of Ca, Fe, O, OH species.

The onset of rusting can also be detected in the laboratory with the use of [ferroxyl indicator solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferroxyl_indicator_solution "Ferroxyl indicator solution"). The solution detects both Fe2+ ions and hydroxyl ions. Formation of Fe2+ ions and hydroxyl ions are indicated by blue and pink patches respectively.

## Prevention

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Rust&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Prevention")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/Uithuizermeeden_de_Boer_02.JPG/250px-Uithuizermeeden_de_Boer_02.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Uithuizermeeden_de_Boer_02.JPG)

[Cor-Ten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weathering_steel "Weathering steel") is a group of steel alloys which were developed to eliminate the need for painting, and form a stable rust-like appearance after several years' exposure to weather.

Because of the widespread use and importance of iron and steel products, and because rusting severely compromises the strength, functionality and the appearance of such products, the prevention and control of rust is the basis of major economic activities in a number of specialized technologies. A brief overview of methods is presented here; for detailed coverage, see the cross-referenced articles.

Rust is [permeable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permeation "Permeation") to air and water, therefore the interior metallic iron beneath a rust layer continues to corrode. Rust prevention thus requires coatings that preclude rust formation.

### Rust-resistant alloys

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Rust&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Rust-resistant alloys")]

See also: [Stainless steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stainless_steel "Stainless steel") and [Weathering steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weathering_steel "Weathering steel")

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/Rust-AH-2022.jpg/250px-Rust-AH-2022.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rust-AH-2022.jpg)

Cor-Ten sheet with rust coating

Stainless steel forms a [passivation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passivation_(chemistry) "Passivation (chemistry)") layer of [chromium(III) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium(III)_oxide "Chromium(III) oxide").[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9) Similar passivation behavior occurs with [magnesium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnesium "Magnesium"), [titanium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanium "Titanium"), [zinc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zinc "Zinc"), [zinc oxides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zinc_oxide "Zinc oxide"), [aluminium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium "Aluminium"), [polyaniline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyaniline "Polyaniline"), and other electroactive conductive polymers.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

Special "[weathering steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weathering_steel "Weathering steel")" alloys such as Cor-Ten rust at a much slower rate than normal, because the rust adheres to the surface of the metal in a protective layer. Designs using this material must include measures that avoid worst-case exposures since the material still continues to rust slowly even under near-ideal conditions.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

### Galvanization

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Rust&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Galvanization")]

Main article: [Galvanization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galvanization "Galvanization")

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Rust_from_bathtub_in_Kyiv.jpg/250px-Rust_from_bathtub_in_Kyiv.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rust_from_bathtub_in_Kyiv.jpg)

Interior rust in old galvanized iron water pipes can result in brown and black water.

Galvanization consists of an application on the object to be protected of a layer of metallic [zinc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zinc "Zinc") by either [hot-dip galvanizing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot-dip_galvanizing "Hot-dip galvanizing") or [electroplating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electroplating "Electroplating"). Zinc is traditionally used because it is cheap, adheres well to steel, and provides [cathodic protection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathodic_protection "Cathodic protection") to the steel surface in case of damage of the zinc layer. In more corrosive environments (such as salt water), [cadmium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadmium "Cadmium") plating is preferred instead of the underlying protected metal. The protective zinc layer is consumed by this action, and thus galvanization provides protection only for a limited period of time.

More modern coatings add aluminium to the coating as *zinc-alume*; aluminium will migrate to cover scratches and thus provide protection for a longer period. These approaches rely on the aluminium and zinc oxides protecting a once-scratched surface, rather than oxidizing as a [sacrificial anode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacrificial_anode "Sacrificial anode") as in traditional galvanized coatings. In some cases, such as very aggressive environments or long design life, both zinc and a [coating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coating "Coating") are applied to provide enhanced corrosion protection.

Typical galvanization of steel products that are to be subjected to normal day-to-day weathering in an outside environment consists of a hot-dipped 85 [μm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Μm "Μm") zinc coating. Under normal weather conditions, this will deteriorate at a rate of 1 μm per year, giving approximately 85 years of protection.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

### Cathodic protection

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Rust&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Cathodic protection")]

Main article: [Cathodic protection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathodic_protection "Cathodic protection")

Cathodic protection is a technique used to inhibit corrosion on buried or immersed structures by supplying an electrical charge that suppresses the electrochemical reaction. If correctly applied, corrosion can be stopped completely. In its simplest form, it is achieved by attaching a sacrificial anode, thereby making the iron or steel the cathode in the cell formed. The sacrificial anode must be made from something with a more negative [electrode potential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrode_potential "Electrode potential") than the iron or steel, commonly zinc, aluminium, or magnesium. The sacrificial anode will eventually corrode away, ceasing its protective action unless it is replaced in a timely manner.

Cathodic protection can also be provided by using an applied electrical current. This would then be known as ICCP Impressed Current Cathodic Protection.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

### Coatings and painting

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Rust&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Coatings and painting")]

Main article: [Rustproofing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustproofing "Rustproofing")

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Flaking_paint_on_rusting_metal.jpg/250px-Flaking_paint_on_rusting_metal.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flaking_paint_on_rusting_metal.jpg)

Flaking paint, exposing a patch of surface rust on sheet metal

Rust formation can be controlled with coatings, such as [paint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paint "Paint"), [lacquer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacquer "Lacquer"), [varnish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varnish "Varnish"), or wax tapes[[14]](#cite_note-14) that isolate the iron from the environment.[[15]](#cite_note-15) Large structures with enclosed box sections, such as ships and modern automobiles, often have a wax-based product (technically a "slushing oil") injected into these sections. Such treatments usually also contain rust inhibitors. Covering steel with concrete can provide some protection to steel because of the [alkaline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkaline "Alkaline") [pH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PH "PH") environment at the steel–concrete interface. However, rusting of steel in concrete can still be a problem, as expanding rust can fracture concrete from within.[[16]](#cite_note-16)[[17]](#cite_note-17)

As a closely related example, iron clamps were used to join [marble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marble "Marble") blocks during a restoration attempt of the [Parthenon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthenon "Parthenon") in [Athens, Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens,_Greece "Athens, Greece"), in 1898, but caused extensive damage to the marble by the rusting and swelling of unprotected iron. The ancient Greek builders had used a similar fastening system for the marble blocks during construction, however, they also poured molten [lead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead "Lead") over the iron joints for protection from seismic shocks as well as from corrosion. This method was successful for the 2500-year-old structure, but in less than a century the crude repairs were in imminent danger of collapse.[[18]](#cite_note-18) When only temporary protection is needed for storage or transport, a thin layer of oil, grease or a special mixture such as [Cosmoline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmoline "Cosmoline") can be applied to an iron surface. Such treatments are extensively used when "[mothballing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reserve_fleet "Reserve fleet")" a steel ship, automobile, or other equipment for long-term storage.

Special anti-seize lubricant mixtures are available and are applied to metallic threads and other precision machined surfaces to protect them from rust. These compounds usually contain grease mixed with copper, zinc, or aluminium powder, and other proprietary ingredients.[[19]](#cite_note-19)

### Bluing

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Rust&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Bluing")]

Main article: [Bluing (steel)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluing_(steel) "Bluing (steel)")

Bluing is a technique that can provide limited [[20]](#cite_note-20) resistance to rusting for small steel items, such as firearms; for it to be successful, a water-displacing oil is rubbed onto the blued steel and other steel.[[21]](#cite_note-21)

### Inhibitors

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Rust&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Inhibitors")]

Main article: [Corrosion inhibitor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corrosion_inhibitor "Corrosion inhibitor")

Corrosion inhibitors, such as gas-phase or volatile inhibitors, can be used to prevent corrosion inside sealed systems. They are not effective when air circulation disperses them, and brings in fresh oxygen and moisture.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

### Humidity control

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Rust&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Humidity control")]

See also: [Dehumidifier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dehumidifier "Dehumidifier") and [Desiccant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desiccant "Desiccant")

Rust can be avoided by controlling the moisture in the atmosphere.[[22]](#cite_note-22) An example of this is the use of [silica gel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silica_gel "Silica gel") packets to control humidity in equipment shipped by sea.

## Treatment

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Rust&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Treatment")]

### Removal

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Rust&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Removal")]

Surface rust can be removed by using [acids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acid "Acid"), [chelating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelation "Chelation") agents, or [sodium hydrosulfite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_hydrosulfite "Sodium hydrosulfite"); or by mechanical action such as scrubbing, [scraping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paint_scraper "Paint scraper"), [sanding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanding "Sanding") or [sand blasting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sand_blasting "Sand blasting"), with or without chemical agents.[[23]](#cite_note-:1-23)

Rust can also be removed using [electrolysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrolysis "Electrolysis"). In a home workshop setting, this can be done using simple materials such as a plastic bucket filled with an electrolyte consisting of [washing soda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_carbonate "Sodium carbonate") dissolved in [tap water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tap_water "Tap water"), a length of [rebar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebar "Rebar") suspended vertically in the solution to act as an [anode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anode "Anode"), another laid across the top of the bucket to act as a support for suspending the object, [baling wire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baling_wire "Baling wire") to suspend the object in the solution from the horizontal rebar, and a [battery charger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battery_charger "Battery charger") as a power source in which the positive terminal is clamped to the anode and the negative terminal is clamped to the object to be treated which becomes the [cathode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathode "Cathode").[[24]](#cite_note-antique-engines-24) Hydrogen and oxygen gases are produced at the cathode and anode respectively. This mixture is flammable/explosive.[[25]](#cite_note-25) Care should also be taken to avoid [hydrogen embrittlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_embrittlement "Hydrogen embrittlement"). Overvoltage also produces small amounts of ozone, which is highly toxic, so a low voltage phone charger is a far safer source of DC current.[[26]](#cite_note-26)

### Conversion

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Rust&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Conversion")]

Rust may be treated with [rust converters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust_converter "Rust converter") - mixtures based on [tannic acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tannic_acid "Tannic acid") or [phosphoric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphoric_acid "Phosphoric acid") which can combine with surface rust to create a protective layer that is ready for painting.[[23]](#cite_note-:1-23)[[27]](#cite_note-27)

## Economic effect

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Rust&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Economic effect")]

Main article: [Corrosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corrosion "Corrosion")

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/Rust_wedge.jpg/250px-Rust_wedge.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rust_wedge.jpg)

Outdoor *Rust Wedge* at the [Exploratorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exploratorium "Exploratorium") showing the expansion of rusting iron

Rust is associated with the degradation of iron-based tools and structures. As rust has a much higher volume than the originating mass of iron, its buildup can also cause failure by forcing apart adjacent parts phenomenon sometimes known as "rust jacking". It was the cause of the collapse of the [Mianus river bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mianus_river_bridge "Mianus river bridge") in 1983, when the bearings rusted internally and pushed one corner of the road slab off its support.

Stress corrosion cracking was responsible for the [Silver Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Bridge "Silver Bridge") disaster of 1967 in [West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Virginia "West Virginia"), when a steel [suspension bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suspension_bridge "Suspension bridge") collapsed in less than a minute, killing 46 drivers and passengers on the bridge at the time. The [Kinzua Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinzua_Bridge "Kinzua Bridge") in [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania") was blown down by a [tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado "Tornado") in 2003, largely because the central base bolts holding the structure to the ground had rusted away, leaving the bridge anchored by gravity alone.

[Reinforced concrete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforced_concrete "Reinforced concrete") is also vulnerable to rust damage. Internal pressure caused by expanding corrosion of concrete-covered steel and iron can cause the concrete to [spall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spall "Spall"), creating severe structural problems. It is one of the most common failure modes of reinforced concrete [bridges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridge "Bridge") and buildings.

## Cultural symbolism

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Rust&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Cultural symbolism")]

Rust is a commonly used [metaphor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metaphor "Metaphor") for slow decay due to neglect, since it gradually converts robust iron and steel metal into a soft crumbling powder. A wide section of the industrialized [American Midwest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Midwest "American Midwest") and [American Northeast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Northeast "American Northeast"), once dominated by [steel foundries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steelmaking "Steelmaking"), the [automotive industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automotive_industry "Automotive industry"), and other manufacturers, has experienced harsh economic cutbacks that have caused the region to be dubbed the "[Rust Belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust_Belt "Rust Belt")".[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

# 5 Different Types of Corrosion Prevention Methods

* by [Tony Collins](https://eoncoat.com/author/tony-collins/ "Posts by Tony Collins")

![corrosion](https://eoncoat.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/shutterstock_518997427.jpg)

We at EonCoat understand the importance of corrosion prevention. Rust and other corrosion forms can lead to safety issues and ruin the integrity of your equipment and supplies. Even routine maintenance to remove and repair corrosion can drive up costs. Fortunately, there are a variety of measures you can take to minimize corrosion. Here we’ll highlight five methods based on cost and effectiveness.

## 1. BARRIER COATINGS

One of the easiest and cheapest ways to prevent corrosion is to use barrier coatings like paint, plastic, or powder. Powders, including epoxy, nylon, and urethane, adhere to the metal surface to create a thin film. Plastic and waxes are often sprayed onto metal surfaces. Paint acts as a coating to protect the metal surface from the electrochemical charge that comes from corrosive compounds. Today’s paint systems are a combination of different paint layers that serve different functions. The primer coat acts as an inhibitor, the intermediate coat adds to the paint’s overall thickness, and the finish coat provides resistance to environmental factors.

The biggest drawback with coatings is that they often need to be stripped and reapplied. Coatings that aren’t applied properly can quickly fail and lead to increased levels of corrosion. Coatings contain volatile organic compounds, which make them hazardous to people and the environment.

---

 ![](https://eoncoat.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/719x488-5.jpg)

*Failing Barrier Coating*

 

---

## 2. HOT-DIP GALVANIZATION

This corrosion prevention method involves dipping steel into molten zinc. The iron in the steel reacts with the zinc to create a tightly bonded alloy coating which serves as protection. The process has been around for more than 250 years and has been used for corrosion protection of things like artistic sculptures and playground equipment.

Unfortunately, [galvanization](https://galvanizeit.org/hot-dip-galvanized-steel-for-parking-structures/hot-dip-galvanizing) can’t be done on-site, meaning companies must pull equipment out of work to be treated. Some equipment may simply be too large for the process, forcing companies to abandon the idea altogether. In addition, zinc can chip or peel. And high exposure to environmental elements can speed up the process of zinc wear, leading to increased maintenance. Lastly, the zinc fumes that release from the galvanizing process are highly toxic.

## 3. ALLOYED STEEL (STAINLESS)

Alloyed steel is one of the most effective corrosion prevention methods around, combining the properties of various metals to provide added strength and resistance to the resulting product. Corrosion-resistant nickel, for example, combined with oxidation-resistant chromium results in an alloy that can be used in oxidized and reduced chemical environments. Different alloys provide resistance to different conditions, giving companies greater flexibility.

Despite its effectiveness, alloyed steel is very expensive.

## 4. CATHODIC PROTECTION

[Cathodic protection protects by electrochemical means](https://eoncoat.com/what-is-cathodic-protection-and-how-does-it-work/). To prevent corrosion, the active sites on the metal surface are converted to passive sites by providing electrons from another source, typically with galvanic anodes attached on or near the surface. Metals used for anodes include aluminum, magnesium, or zinc.

While cathodic protection is highly effective, anodes get used up and need to be checked and/or replaced often which can drive up costs of maintenance. They also increase the weight of the attached structure and aren’t always effective in high-resistivity environments.

---

 ![](https://eoncoat.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/12/719x488-8.jpg)

*Pipeline using Cathodic Protection*

 

---

## 5. EONCOAT – A NEW WAY TO PROTECT ASSETS FROM CORROSION

Choosing the right corrosion prevention for your equipment isn’t easy. Each of the above methods has its pros and cons. [EonCoat](https://eoncoat.com/eoncoat-science-technology/) is a cost-effective, maintenance-free, and easily applied solution which protects the life of the asset. It works by a combination of the above methods. First, it alloys the metal, then provides a thick layer of inhibitors that will repair any damage to the alloy layer. EonCoat uses no toxic chemicals and has no VOC’s so it is the most environmentally friendly solution. Independent testing shows this solution to be the most effective and long-lasting of all the alternatives. The 30-year warranty ensures your equipment stays protected. *Methods of Corrosion Control and Protection*  

Corrosion is the gradual deterioration of metals due to chemical or electrochemical reactions with the environment. Various methods are used to control and prevent corrosion, depending on the material, environment, and application.  

---

*1. Protective Coatings & Paints*  
*Barrier Coatings* – Paints, epoxies, or polymers create a physical barrier between the metal and the environment.  
*Galvanization* – A zinc coating (hot-dip or electroplating) protects steel from rusting.  
*Powder Coating* – A dry powder applied and cured to form a durable, corrosion-resistant layer.  

---

*2. Cathodic Protection (CP)*  
*Sacrificial Anode Method* – Uses a more reactive metal (e.g., zinc, magnesium, or aluminum) to corrode instead of the protected metal.  
*Impressed Current Cathodic Protection (ICCP)* – An external power source supplies current to counteract corrosion, commonly used in pipelines and marine structures.  

---

*3. Corrosion Inhibitors*  
Chemicals added to the environment to slow down corrosion.  
*Types:*  
*Anodic Inhibitors* – Form protective oxide layers (e.g., chromates).  
*Cathodic Inhibitors* – Reduce hydrogen evolution (e.g., sulfites).  
*Volatile Corrosion Inhibitors (VCIs)* – Used in enclosed spaces like pipelines and storage tanks.  

---

*4. Material Selection & Alloying*  
Using *corrosion-resistant materials* like stainless steel, titanium, or corrosion-resistant alloys (CRAs).  
Adding elements like chromium, nickel, and molybdenum enhances corrosion resistance.  

---

*5. Environmental Modification*  
*Reducing humidity* in storage areas.  
*Controlling pH levels* in industrial processes.  
*Removing corrosive agents* like chloride, oxygen, and sulfur compounds from the environment.  

---

*6. Proper Design & Maintenance*  
Avoiding crevices where moisture can accumulate.  
Using *drainage holes* to prevent water accumulation.  
*Regular inspections* to detect and address early corrosion.  

---

*7. Electroplating & Anodizing*  
*Electroplating* – Depositing a metal layer (e.g., nickel, chrome) on the surface to enhance corrosion resistance.  
*Anodizing* – Forms a protective oxide layer, commonly used for aluminum.  

---

*8. Corrosion-Resistant Linings*  
Rubber, plastic, or ceramic linings inside tanks and pipes protect against aggressive chemicals.  

---
